newsitem.title: USA: IPO SPOTLIGHT - India's BPL makes US debut.
newsitem.headline: IPO SPOTLIGHT - India's BPL makes US debut.

text.p: BPL Cellular Holdings Ltd's filing to list American depositary shares (ADR) on the Nasdaq breaks new ground for Indian companies, traditionally associated with global depositary receipt (GDR) offerings, which require less disclosure and are less expensive.
The IPO is viewed cautiously by analysts, who cite the wireless telecommunications services provider's shaky financial performance and political uncertainty in India.
"The deal will get done on the strength of the underwriter, but without much fanfare in the after-market," said David Menlow, president of Springfield, N.J.-based IPO Financial Network.
Menlow said the timing of the IPO was off with the approach of the huge Deutsche Telekom deal and the Venezuelan telephone company CANTV's public offering, both due next week.

BPL Cellular, which started commercial operations in October 1995, reported operating revenue of $7.7 million for the fiscal year ended March 31,1996, and a net loss of $117 million. According to the prospectus, it expects to generate losses for the next three years at least.

In partnership with France Telecom, it is one of two digital mobile operators in Bombay. Under its joint venture with U S West Communications Group, it holds licenses for cellular services in three of India's more developed states - Maharashtra, of which Bombay is the capital, and the southern states of Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
It also provides paging services in the cities of Cochin and Trivandrum, and holds paging licenses for three states.
Sheriar Irani, an analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities in Bombay, said the telecom industry in India is in its early days.
"The industry is in a nascent stage," he said. "It will be a couple of years before you can tell how things are really going."

Analysts had a cautiously upbeat view of the industry going forward. "The first six months in the four cities got off to a slow start (as) import duties were high and handsets very expensive" said Ayesha Ahmad, senior associate at Cambridge, Mass.-based Pyramid Research. "We believe growth will pick up in the next year or two as handset prices fall."

In the final analysis, market observers said, the success of BPL's IPO depended on the pricing. "At the end of the day," said Irani, "it's what sort of valuation is being thrown about" in the United States.

Other Indian telecom companies are gearing up to follow BPL's lead. Hutchison Max Telecom last week got the nod from the Indian government for a $150 million ADR issue. The company is a joint venture between the Hong Kong-based telecommunications group Hutchison Whampoa Ltd and Max India Ltd. .
Another telecom group, Bharati Televentures Ltd, is also seeking approval for an ADR issue, according to Indian media reports.

BPL Cellular said in its filing that it planned to use about $125 million of the proceeds as funding for its subsidiaries, to purchase equipment and build its networks. It will use about $56.2 million to repay debt.
After the IPO, affiliates of the BPL Group - an Indian business group of which BPL Cellular is a unit - will own about 78 percent of BPL Cellular's shares. ---New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610
